article.title: Causal Inference When Randomization Is Not Available
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: Randomized experiments are powerful because random assignment breaks the systematic relationship between treatment and pre-treatment characteristics, allowing differences in outcomes to be interpreted causally under a clear design. In many business settings, however, randomization is unavailable. A policy may already have been launched, treatment may be determined by customer choice, or operational and ethical constraints may prevent withholding an intervention. Analysts then turn to observational causal inference. The challenge is confounding. Treated and untreated units may differ for reasons that also affect the outcome. Customers who receive a premium service, for example, may already be higher-value customers. Simply comparing their later spending with other customers mixes treatment effect with pre-existing differences. Matching attempts to construct a comparison group with similar observed characteristics. Propensity-score methods summarize the estimated probability of treatment given observed covariates and can support matching, stratification, or weighting. Inverse-probability weighting creates a pseudo-population in which measured covariates are more balanced across treatment groups. These approaches rely on a demanding assumption: after conditioning on the measured variables, there are no important unmeasured confounders. Good balance after weighting does not prove that assumption. Difference-in-differences uses a different source of identification. It compares changes over time between treated and comparison groups, removing time-invariant group differences. Its key parallel-trends assumption is that, without treatment, the groups would have followed similar trends. Analysts should inspect pre-treatment trends and consider events that affect the groups differently. Fixed-effects models can control for stable unit characteristics, but they do not automatically remove time-varying confounding. Regression discontinuity can be compelling when treatment is assigned by a threshold, such as eligibility above a score or age cutoff. Units just above and below the threshold may be comparable, allowing a local causal estimate if manipulation around the cutoff is limited and other factors change smoothly. Instrumental-variable methods can address some unmeasured confounding when a valid instrument changes treatment exposure but affects the outcome only through treatment. Valid instruments are difficult to justify, and weak instruments can produce unstable estimates. No observational method creates causality merely by using sophisticated mathematics. Identification comes from assumptions about how the data were generated. Those assumptions should be stated before presenting an estimate. Analysts should define the treatment, outcome, target population, time zero, covariates measured before treatment, and causal contrast of interest. They should avoid controlling for mediators or variables caused by treatment because doing so can introduce bias. Diagnostics are essential: inspect overlap, covariate balance, pre-trends where relevant, sensitivity to model specification, and robustness to alternative definitions. Negative controls or sensitivity analyses can reveal whether conclusions depend heavily on untestable assumptions. The language of the result should match the design. A randomized experiment may support a direct causal statement under its assumptions. An observational study should explain the identification strategy and its limitations rather than simply calling an adjusted association an effect. Business decisions rarely require perfect certainty, but they do require clarity about what would have to be true for the estimate to represent a causal effect. When randomization is unavailable, causal inference is not about finding a statistical technique that replaces experimentation. It is about constructing a credible comparison, making assumptions explicit, testing what can be tested, and showing decision makers how sensitive the conclusion is to what cannot be observed. Analysts should state the population, observation window, assumptions, and decision point before interpreting the result. A useful review separates the observed pattern from the mechanism that may have produced it and from the action that should follow. This discipline makes the analysis easier to reproduce, challenge, and communicate to stakeholders. paragraphs.zh: 繁中完整翻譯與解說：本文重點是不要讓單一摘要數字、留下來的樣本、模型選擇結果或統計調整取代對資料生成機制的理解。分析時要先界定母體、時間點、selection mechanism 與真正要回答的 business question，再判斷觀察到的差異可以支持到什麼程度。
paragraphs.ja: 日本語完全訳・解説：単一の要約値、生き残ったsample、modelによるselection、統計的な調整だけでdata generating processを置き換えて考えないことが重要である。母集団、時点、selection mechanism、business questionを先に定義し、観察された差がどこまでの結論を支持できるかを判断する。
